newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Wheat prices down on U.S. rain.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Wheat prices down on U.S. rain.

text.p: Wheat prices dropped on U.S. markets on Monday after good weekend rains swept dry farm regions of the United States.

Benchmark Chicago Board of Trade July wheat futures were lower by 7-1/2 cents per bushel toward mid-session at $3.45 on news that there had been generous rainfall, especially in the key spring wheat state of North Dakota.
Big players FIMAT Futures, E.D. and F. Man International and Rand Financial each sold roughly one half million bushels of July wheat, traders in Chicago said.
Minneapolis and Kansas City wheat futures also traded lower as much-needed rains fell on dry wheat growing regions of North Dakota.

"The high pressure ridge that has been blocking moisture has been defeated, and rain showers can go forward -- not unlike the weather pattern we saw earlier this year in northern France," a trader said.

Chicago soybean futures also opened sharply lower on nearly ideal crop weather including rain and warmer temperatures in the U.S. Midwest and on renewed talk the U.S. may import soybeans, traders said.
July soybeans were soon down 10 cents at $8.44-1/2 a bushel.
Activity was subdued in most other world commodity markets.
Coffee prices were mixed after falling briskly on Friday ahead of a report by the U.S. Agriculture Department on the size of the coffee crop in Brazil, the top world producer.
The report, released after the futures market closed, stunned traders by projecting Brazil's harvest at 28 million (60 kg) bags, up from 27.5 million a year earlier.

"What is the most shocking thing is to say there is more coming this year than last. That is totally wrong," Jorge Esteve, president of the Brazilian Coffee Exporters Association, said in Rio de Janeiro.
A recent rally in coffee, to a 20-year high in New York, was driven by concerns about tight Latin American supply.
London robusta coffee futures trimmed losses to end the day down just $7 on the September contract at $1,778 per tonne.
Cocoa was also mixed after advancing in New York on Friday to the highest in eight years.
Fund speculators bought cocoa last week on concerns about next season's crop in top producer Ivory Coast and worries about a developing El Nino weather pattern.
The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said ocean temperatures in the South Pacific were the highest since August 1983, with an El Nino effect in progress.
In the past, dryness in the southern hemisphere has been one result of El Nino. The 1983 El Nino caused severe drought in Indonesia, the world's third-largest cocoa producer.
But London cocoa futures were seen consolidating on Monday after the rally. They eased by five pounds sterling to a close at 1,123 pounds for September.
Industrial metals were barely changed in dull trading on the London Metal Exchange. Crude oil also traded within a range.
And the gold market slumbered through Monday while platinum and palladium ticked marginally lower on light New York-led selling.
Bullion was fixed in London at $341.50 an ounce compared $341.40 on Friday afternoon.

Merrill Lynch analyst Ted Arnold said at the annual Financial Times gold conference in Prague that the world gold price was more likely to fall to $250 an ounce within the next 24 months than climb to $450.00.
